strengths: Solid theoretical derivation of the exact tall-data posterior score decomposition (Section 3.1) with a rigorous Gaussian-kernel approximation (Lemmas 3.1/3.2, with full proofs in the appendix) that yields a principled, sound alternative to prior Langevin-based approaches.

Avoids the need for MCMC/Langevin sampling to combine individual-observation scores into a tall-data posterior score, enabling use of fast deterministic samplers like DDIM; this is a meaningful methodological advance over F-NPSE (Geffner et al., 2023).

Extensive and diverse experimental validation: analytically tractable Gaussian/GMM toy models with controlled score-error injection, three SBI benchmark tasks of increasing dimensionality, a real neuroscience simulator (JRNMM), and additional benchmark tasks in the appendix (multimodal, high-dimensional, non-Gaussian priors).
Careful empirical analysis of computational cost (neural network evaluations, wall-clock time) showing consistent speedups (~5x) at equal or better accuracy relative to the Langevin baseline.

Transparent discussion of limitations, including instability of the Jacobian-based (JAC) variant, sensitivity of Langevin sampling to step-size choice (Appendix J), and accumulation of approximation error with increasing number of observations (evidenced by MMD trends).

Useful additional analyses (classifier-free guidance for learning prior scores, partial factorization trade-off) that strengthen practical applicability and show the authors probed the boundaries of their method.
weaknesses: The core approximation (constant/Gaussian covariance for backward kernels) is a heuristic with no formal bound on the resulting bias in the estimated tall-data posterior score, especially for non-Gaussian or multimodal posteriors; the paper relies solely on empirical validation.

Performance is inconsistent across tasks: e.g., in the GMM (uniform prior) additional benchmark, GAUSS is clearly worse than LANGEVIN (Fig. 16), and JAC is unusable without ad hoc clipping stabilization in most non-toy settings, undermining claims of general superiority.

MMD results (Section 4.2, Appendix H.2) show increasing error with the number of observations n for all methods including GAUSS, indicating unresolved error accumulation that is only partially mitigated via the partial-factorization extension relegated to the appendix.

The main empirical baseline is limited to F-NPSE/Langevin; augmented NPE/NLE/NRE baselines are excluded (justified by prior literature but reduces the comprehensiveness of the comparison), and the Langevin baseline had to be reimplemented since the original authors' code was unavailable, introducing some uncertainty about comparison fidelity.
The 'equivalent time setting' used to compare methods (different step counts per method) could introduce a hyperparameter-selection bias favoring the proposed samplers.

Dense notation and heavy reliance on appendix material (many key clarifications, e.g., positive-definiteness conditions for Λ(θ), correction-term behavior, are deferred there) reduce self-containedness and readability of the main text.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated practical problem (tall-data SBI) and clearly identifies the drawback of the leading baseline (F-NPSE's reliance on annealed Langevin dynamics, which is sensitive to step size and slow).

Solid theoretical derivation: the exact factorization of the tall-data posterior score (Section 3.1) and the second-order Gaussian approximation with detailed proofs (Lemmas 3.1, 3.2, Appendix A) give a principled justification for the proposed GAUSS/JAC algorithms.

Broad experimental scope: toy Gaussian/GMM models with analytic ground truth, three SBI benchmark tasks, additional benchmark tasks in the appendix (Gaussian Linear, GMM, B-GLM, Two Moons), and a real non-linear neuroscience model (JRNMM), plus useful ablations (equivalent-time comparisons, tamed ULA comparison, CFG and partial-factorization extensions).

Demonstrated computational advantages: GAUSS achieves comparable or better sample quality than Langevin-based F-NPSE with roughly 5x fewer network evaluations in the reported settings, which is a meaningful practical benefit if it holds robustly.
Reasonably detailed implementation/appendix documentation (architecture, training, model-selection strategy, evaluation metrics) that aids reproducibility, modulo the missing code link.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core approximation (constant/Gaussian covariance Tweedie projection) is a direct application of Boys et al. (2023)'s existing technique to the tall-data SBI factorized-score setting of Geffner et al. (2023); the contribution is largely a combination/adaptation rather than a fundamentally new idea.

The positive-definiteness requirement on Λ(θ), which underlies the validity of the GAUSS/JAC score approximation, is not guaranteed in general; Appendix B's discussion concludes that a 'sufficient' condition would require the prior to be more concentrated than the posterior, which the authors themselves note 'does not make much sense' — this leaves a real theoretical gap unaddressed in the main text.

JAC, one of the two proposed algorithms, is reported to diverge for essentially any perturbation or on all SBI benchmark tasks without ad hoc clipping, undermining confidence in the generality/robustness of the proposed framework beyond the specific GAUSS heuristic.

Internal inconsistency in the results: while sliced-Wasserstein distances generally improve or stay flat with more observations n, the MMD metric (Appendix H.2, Figs. 12–13) shows *increasing* error with n for GAUSS across all three benchmark tasks, directly contradicting the paper's central narrative that the method scales gracefully with the number of observations and avoids error accumulation compared to F-NPSE.

Additional benchmark results (Appendix I) show mixed outcomes (e.g., GMM (uniform), B-GLM raw) where GAUSS is not clearly superior to Langevin or JAC, tempering the paper's claim of 'superiority... on several numerical experiments.'

The comparison is restricted to a single competing baseline (F-NPSE); other tall-data approaches (augmented NPE/NLE/NRE) are excluded based on prior literature rather than being re-validated in this specific experimental setup, narrowing the empirical support for the claimed superiority.

The neuroscience JRNMM application lacks ground-truth posterior comparison (relying only on MMD-to-Dirac against the true simulating parameter), which is a weaker form of validation than the benchmark tasks with MCMC references.
The code repository link in the manuscript appears to be a placeholder/empty, raising concerns about verifiability of the reproducibility claims at submission time.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy, which may hinder accessibility; some of the theoretical exposition (e.g., handling of F(θ,x) terms, conditions for exactness) is deferred to lengthy appendices, making it hard to assess the practical scope of the approximation from the main text alone.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: extending score-based SBI (NPSE) to the tall-data setting without requiring an augmented training dataset or MCMC/Langevin sampling at inference time.

Solid theoretical contribution: the paper derives an exact decomposition of the diffused tall-data posterior score (Section 3.1) and then a tractable second-order Gaussian approximation (Lemma 3.1, 3.2, proofs in Appendix A) that reduces to a simple linear-solve combination of individual posterior scores.
Two concrete, easy-to-implement algorithms (GAUSS and JAC) are provided with pseudocode, and their trade-offs (speed vs. stability vs. dimensionality scaling) are clearly articulated.

Extensive and well-designed experimental suite: analytically tractable Gaussian/GMM toy models (allowing decoupling of score error via the epsilon-perturbation trick), three SBI benchmark tasks of increasing complexity, and a real non-linear neuroscience application (JRNMM) with physically interpretable results (indeterminacy in mu, sigma vs g).

Demonstrated practical benefits: GAUSS is shown to be both faster (fewer NNEs) and more numerically stable than the F-NPSE/Langevin baseline across most settings, which is a meaningful and useful contribution to the SBI toolbox.

Strong supplementary material: additional benchmark tasks (Two Moons, GMM, B-GLM), classifier-free guidance extension for cases lacking analytic prior score, and a partial-factorization extension, along with a careful diagnosis of Langevin's sensitivity to step-size and score-model quality (Appendix J).

Honest treatment of limitations, e.g., JAC's poor scaling with dimension and instability under noisy scores, and the increasing MMD with more observations n due to error accumulation, rather than hiding these results.
weaknesses: The empirical comparison is limited to F-NPSE only; while the authors justify excluding augmented NPE/NLE/NRE by citing prior work, this narrows the range of baselines tested in this specific paper.

The core GAUSS approximation relies on a Gaussian/second-order approximation of the backward kernels, which is exact only in the Gaussian case; for non-Gaussian posteriors (GMM, SBI benchmark tasks) there is no theoretical error bound on the approximation quality, and the paper relies solely on empirical validation.

MMD results (Section 4.2/Appendix H) show a generally increasing error with n, attributed to compounding score-approximation errors from repeated network evaluations; this could limit scalability to very large tall-data settings, which is only partially addressed via the appendix's partial factorization extension.

Reproduction of the F-NPSE baseline uses a best-effort reimplementation since the original authors' code is unavailable (noted in Appendix J), introducing some uncertainty into the head-to-head comparisons.

JAC is reported to scale poorly with parameter dimension m and to require unstable Jacobian computations, limiting its practical applicability; its inclusion as a main method (vs. relegating it to an ablation) is somewhat inconsistent with these acknowledged drawbacks.

The paper is dense with heavy notation and appendix-dependent derivations, and central results (e.g., Lemma 3.1/3.2, positive-definiteness conditions on Λ(θ)) require substantial appendix cross-referencing, which may reduce accessibility for a broader ICML audience.

The classifier-free guidance extension for learning the prior score shows degraded performance under discontinuous (Uniform) priors, suggesting the approach's applicability to more general prior classes needs further development.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem: efficient sampling from tall-data posteriors in simulation-based inference without retraining or augmented simulation budgets.

Provides a principled theoretical derivation (Lemmas 3.1 and 3.2, with full proofs in the appendix) expressing the tall-data posterior score in terms of single-observation posterior scores and prior scores, clarifying exactly which term (the missing normalizing/coupling term) is neglected by the prior F-NPSE approach.
Proposes two concrete algorithmic instantiations (GAUSS and JAC) with a clear discussion of their respective trade-offs (computational cost, stability, dimensionality scaling).

Extensive and diverse empirical evaluation: controlled toy Gaussian/GMM models with analytic ground truth and controllable score error, standard SBI benchmark tasks (SLCP, SIR, Lotka-Volterra plus several additional tasks in the appendix), and a real computational neuroscience application (JRNMM) evaluated with the principled ℓ-C2ST diagnostic.

Good empirical rigor: multiple complementary metrics (sliced Wasserstein, MMD, C2ST), analysis of speed vs. accuracy trade-offs under an 'equivalent time' comparison protocol, and thoughtful additional studies of Langevin step-size sensitivity, classifier-free guidance for implicit prior scores, and partial factorization to control error accumulation.

Demonstrates the practical benefit of the approach directly: GAUSS is consistently faster and more numerically stable than the Langevin-based F-NPSE baseline, particularly as the number of observations n grows.

Honest limitations discussion, including failure cases for both baseline and proposed methods on harder benchmark tasks (Appendix I) and a discussion of the instability of the Jacobian-based approximation.
Code and experimental details (architectures, training protocols, hyperparameters) are provided, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core approximation (Gaussian backward kernels, Section 3.2) is only exact in the Gaussian case; for general (non-Gaussian) posteriors it is a heuristic without formal error bounds or convergence guarantees, and the paper does not theoretically characterize when/why it should be accurate.

The JAC variant is shown to be unstable in most non-trivial settings and requires an ad hoc 'clipping' fix to be usable, which undercuts the motivation for introducing it as a competing second-order approximation; its practical value in the paper's own experiments is limited.

Results in Appendix I reveal that on several harder/more structured benchmark tasks (e.g., Two Moons, B-GLM raw) all methods, including the proposed GAUSS, fail according to the C2ST diagnostic, raising open questions about the general scalability and reliability of the method that are somewhat under-addressed in the main text.

The positive-definiteness condition on Λ(θ) required for the method to be well-defined (Appendix B) is only sketched with a sufficient heuristic condition; no discussion of how often/when it might fail in practice or how failures are handled numerically.

Comparisons are restricted to F-NPSE as the sole competing tall-data baseline (augmented NPE/NLE/NRE excluded by appeal to prior literature); while reasonably justified, this narrows the empirical comparison to a single alternative and limits the strength of the 'superiority' claims made in the abstract.

The additional cost of estimating Σ0,j per observation via a preliminary short DDIM run (100 steps) for GAUSS is not fully incorporated into the reported timing comparisons, which could slightly overstate the speed advantage.

The accumulation of approximation error with increasing n (evident in MMD/C2ST curves in the appendix) is acknowledged but only partially mitigated via the partial factorization extension, which itself introduces an additional hyperparameter (n_max) without clear guidance on how to select it a priori.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuine and practically important gap: existing tall-data SBI extensions (F-NPSE) rely on Langevin dynamics that are sensitive to step-size/number-of-steps choices, and the authors give a principled derivation (Lemmas 3.1/3.2, with full proofs in Appendix A) of a DDIM-compatible score decomposition for the tall posterior that avoids MCMC-style sampling.

The empirical evaluation is extensive: two analytically tractable toy models (Gaussian, GMM) with controllable score-estimation error, three standard SBI-benchmark tasks, additional benchmark tasks in the appendix (Two Moons, B-GLM, GMM-uniform, Gaussian Linear), and a real computational-neuroscience application (Jansen-Rit neural mass model), together with wall-clock timing comparisons.

Reproducibility is well addressed: a released code repository, detailed hyperparameter/architecture description, model-selection procedure with diagnostic plots (Appendix E, F), and pre-computed results for fast reproduction.

The authors are transparent about several limitations of their own proposal (e.g., JAC's dependence on a potentially unstable Jacobian, need for clipping, accumulation of errors with n, failure cases in Appendix I), and provide auxiliary studies (classifier-free guidance for the prior score, partial factorization) that meaningfully explore mitigations.
The impact statement and positive-definiteness analysis (Appendix B) and diffusion-time analysis of the correction term (Appendix C) show attention to correctness and robustness of the approximation.
weaknesses: The headline second-order approximation (GAUSS) is only exact for exactly Gaussian posteriors; for every non-Gaussian case studied (GMM, SBI benchmark tasks, JRNMM) it is an uncontrolled heuristic with no theoretical error bound, so the core methodological claim rests entirely on empirical validation rather than analysis, weakening soundness.

JAC, one of the two central algorithmic proposals, is shown to diverge in essentially all non-trivial settings (n>1) in the main SBI benchmark experiments and needs an additional, undermotivated 'clipping' hack to be usable at all, which is a substantial failure of the paper's own second contribution.

The paper's own text concedes that 'all samplers fail to accurately infer the tall posterior in more complex data settings' (Section 4.2, Appendix I), and the harder C2ST metric (Appendix H.3, I) shows values near 1.0 (near-total distinguishability from the truth) for GAUSS, JAC, and LANGEVIN alike in several benchmark tasks (Two Moons, B-GLM raw, SIR at higher n), which considerably undercuts the claimed 'superiority' that is emphasized mainly through the less discriminative sliced-Wasserstein metric.

Errors are shown to accumulate with increasing number of observations n (Appendix H), which is a fundamental scalability concern for the tall-data setting that motivates the paper; the proposed remedy (partial factorization, Appendix L.2) reintroduces the augmented-training/simulation-budget trade-offs the paper originally sought to avoid, diluting the central selling point of using only a single-observation-trained score network.

Comparisons are restricted to F-NPSE; augmented NPE/NLE/NRE baselines are excluded based on citations to prior work rather than direct empirical comparison in this specific tall-data regime, leaving the completeness of the empirical case for the method's advantage less than fully established.

The dimensionality tested for JAC/GAUSS is modest (m ≤ 20 in the benchmark tasks, m ≤ 32 in toy studies); JAC is explicitly noted as prohibitive for large m, and no experiments probe scalability of GAUSS to higher-dimensional parameter spaces where the constant-covariance approximation may degrade further.

The manuscript structure heavily front-loads dense theory in the main text while relegating most of the decisive empirical evidence (including several failure modes) to a very long appendix (~40 pages), making the main paper less self-contained and potentially obscuring how narrow the settings are in which the method convincingly outperforms alternatives.

strengths: The paper addresses an important gap in SBI: sampling from tall data posteriors using score-based diffusion without relying on unstable/expensive Langevin dynamics, extending the F-NPSE framework of Geffner et al. (2023) in a principled way.

The theoretical derivation is careful and rigorous: the exact decomposition of the tall posterior score into individual posterior scores plus a correction term (Lemma 3.1, 3.2) is well justified, with full proofs provided in the appendix, and the paper correctly identifies that this correction term is what F-NPSE neglects (explaining its dependence on Langevin dynamics).

Two practical approximations (GAUSS and JAC) are proposed with clear derivations connecting to prior work (Boys et al., 2023; Song et al., 2023), and a clean algorithmic description (Algorithms 1-2) is provided, aiding reproducibility.

The experimental evaluation is extensive: controlled Gaussian/GMM toy problems with known analytic posteriors and controllable score error, three SBI benchmark tasks with multiple metrics (sW, MMD, C2ST), a real neuroscience application (JRNMM) validated via ℓ-C2ST, and a very thorough appendix with additional benchmark tasks, ablations on step-size sensitivity of Langevin sampling, classifier-free guidance for non-analytic priors, and partial factorization trade-offs.

GAUSS is shown to be both faster (fewer effective network evaluations per step) and empirically more robust/accurate than the Langevin baseline across nearly all tested settings, which is a meaningful practical contribution.
Code and implementation details (architecture, training, hyperparameter selection strategy) are thoroughly documented, supporting reproducibility.

Honest treatment of limitations: the paper acknowledges JAC's instability, the failure of all methods on some difficult benchmark tasks (e.g., Two Moons, B-GLM raw in appendix I), and the error accumulation issue with increasing n, rather than overselling results.
weaknesses: The core approximation (Gaussian backward kernels, Section 3.2) is only exact in the Gaussian case; for more complex/multimodal posteriors (e.g., GMM, or real-world tasks) the quality of the approximation is unclear beyond empirical checks, and no theoretical error bounds or convergence guarantees are given for GAUSS under general (non-Gaussian) posteriors.

The paper's central comparison is against a single baseline, F-NPSE (Langevin-based), reproduced by the authors since the original code is not available; this introduces risk that the Langevin baseline is not optimally tuned, despite the appendix's effort to address this concern (Appendix K).

Positive definiteness of the matrix Λ(θ), required for the method to be valid, is not guaranteed in general (Appendix B only gives a sufficient heuristic condition based on prior covariance dominance), and it's unclear how often/severely this is violated in practice or how the algorithm behaves when it is.

Scalability limitations are acknowledged but not fully resolved: results in Appendix I show all methods (including GAUSS) fail on harder tasks (Two Moons, B-GLM raw), and error accumulates with increasing n (Appendix H), somewhat undermining the tall-data motivation for large n regimes without the partial factorization workaround.

The method still requires n separate evaluations of the score network per diffusion step (plus optional covariance estimation via mini-DDIM runs for GAUSS), so while faster than Langevin, the per-step cost still scales linearly with n and could be costly for very large n or high-dimensional θ (the JAC approach explicitly does not scale to large m due to the Jacobian computation).

Minor presentation issues: the paper is dense with heavy notation, and some of the appendix material (e.g., partial factorization, classifier-free guidance) that seems fairly important for practical usability is relegated entirely to appendices rather than integrated into the main text.
